questions.prompt: Explain what 'the data model is data' means mechanically in Twenty's server: when a workspace admin adds a custom field, which rows get written, what physical change happens in Postgres, in what order and under which transaction, and what stops the change before anything is written?

keyPoints.text: [w2] The motivation: with a compile-time model, customer-defined fields end up as generic spare columns or a blob, and every filter, sort, permission and webhook treats them worse than built-in data.

[w3] The field service does not write anything directly: it turns the input into a desired flat entity and calls validateBuildAndRunWorkspaceMigration; the builder diffs desired against current flat maps, and a failed validation returns status 'fail', which the service throws as a WorkspaceMigrationBuilderException before the runner is ever called.

[w3] The create-field handler has two halves run on the same queryRunner: executeForMetadata inserts the fieldMetadata rows, and executeForWorkspaceSchema resolves the workspace's schema and table and issues the column DDL there, so the row and the column commit or roll back together.
[w2] A relation field is one action that creates both sides: the action carries the related field's definition, and ids are minted for both before they are written.

[w2] The runner opens one transaction for all actions of the migration and folds each handler's partial optimistic cache into its working maps, so later actions in the same run see what earlier ones created.
[w2] An operator switch, WORKSPACE_SCHEMA_DDL_LOCKED, makes the runner refuse every metadata migration (used during hot upgrades), because each one is also schema DDL.
[w1] When the diff produces no actions the call returns success without opening a transaction, so re-submitting an already-applied definition is a no-op.

questions.prompt: Walk through how a committed metadata change in Twenty reaches the caches of every server instance: what the runner refreshes and in what order, how another instance notices, and where a request, or the next migration, can still work from an outdated picture of the metadata.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The refresh happens only after COMMIT, never inside the transaction: the runner first flushes the flat-entity maps the run touched and then fires the dependent refreshes, so for a moment the database is ahead of every cache.

[w3] The next migration also starts from the cache: the runner loads the flat maps for the actions' metadata, plus their related, relation and validation-related names, through getOrRecompute before it opens its transaction, so a change can be validated and applied against a picture this instance has not refreshed yet.

[w2] After a run touching object or field maps, the runner increments the metadata version, flushes the cached find-all-views operation, and invalidates and recomputes the role, permission, ORM-entity and resolver-name caches.

[w3] getOrRecompute is tiered: an in-process entry is trusted for 100 ms, then its hash is compared with the Redis hash; a mismatch pulls data from Redis, and a Redis miss recomputes from the provider and stores the result under a fresh random UUID hash, which is how other instances detect the change.

[w2] invalidateAndRecompute flushes Redis and the local entry, recomputes, and clears the promise memoizer both before and after, so readers that raced the flush window do not keep an old result on this instance.

[w3] If invalidation fails after the transaction has committed, the runner only logs it: the field exists in Postgres and in the metadata rows, the caller is told success, and the caches can keep describing the previous schema until something else refreshes them.

[w1] The dependent refreshes run side by side under Promise.allSettled, so one failing cache does not stop the others; the runner then raises a single error counting the failures, which the post-commit path only logs.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict the decision to make Twenty's data model runtime data rather than a fixed schema with a JSONB custom-fields column or a per-tenant code-generation-and-redeploy pipeline. Use what a metadata change costs and what a failed one leaves behind at this commit.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Against the JSONB column, the code buys real types per field: a select, multi-select or rating field first gets its own Postgres enum type, and then every column is generated from the field definition and added to that workspace's table, in the same transaction.

[w2] Against generate-and-redeploy: a change to the standard model still reaches each workspace as data, because the standard application's sync diffs its code-defined maps against that workspace's maps and runs the result as a migration with isSystemBuild switched on, so a deploy ships definitions, not DDL.
[w2] Ordinary edits run with isSystemBuild off, so a system object accepts only standardOverrides and isActive changes from an admin; only the standard sync may rewrite it.

[w3] A failed run is contained by the database rollback alone: the runner rolls the transaction back and then calls each action's rollback handler in reverse order, but at this commit every handler inherits a no-op rollbackForMetadata, and the error is rethrown as a WorkspaceMigrationRunnerException (INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR for unknown causes).

[w2] Because metadata inserts and DDL share that one transaction on the field path, half-applied DDL is not the usual failure here; the gaps sit outside it, in cache invalidation and in the metadata events emitted after the run.

[w2] The standard sync also deletes: it runs with inferDeletionFromMissingEntities over the entities the standard application owns, so whatever the code stops defining becomes delete actions in every workspace on its next sync, while custom entities are outside the comparison.

[w1] Changes cascade through metadata, not just columns: deleting a field also deletes or updates the indexes that use it and deletes page-layout widgets configured on that field, all in the same migration request.

[w1] Even a refused change costs a cache flush: after a rollback the runner invalidates the same cache keys it would after a commit, and only logs if that fails, so a failed edit can still evict the warm metadata other instances were using.
